title: An intrasplenic injection model of pancreatic cancer metastasis to the liver in mice
protocol: Anesthetize mice via isoflurane inhalation.
Place the mouse in an anesthesia chamber with 2% isoflurane delivered with 2% oxygen.
Maintain body temperature by placing the anesthesia chamber on top of an electrical heat pad.
Monitor the mouse closely and remove once consciousness is lost.
Administer a small amount of eye ointment to avoid corneal drying and trauma.
Transfer the mouse to the aseptic surgical area.
Maintain anesthetization with 2% isoflurane with 2% oxygen delivered via nose-cone.
Position the mouse in a lateral position on its right side for intrasplenic injection of tumor cells.
Shave fur along the torso of the mouse.
Clean the skin with 80% ethanol.
Wipe the site of fur removal with gauze soaked in 2% Chlorhexidine.
Wipe the area again with 80% ethanol.
Dry the skin with a clean piece of gauze.
Palpate the region just below the ribs and make a single subcostal incision (approximately 1.5 cm) to access the peritoneal cavity.
Gently expose the spleen and associated splenic ligaments using forceps.
Place a dry square of gauze underneath the organ to hold it in place.
Resuspend KPC pancreatic cancer cells by gently pipetting up and down.
Draw up 50 μL of cancer cells in a Hamilton syringe, ensuring no air bubbles are present.
Gently insert the tip of the needle (3 mm) into the spleen.
Slowly inject cancer cells over a period of 40 seconds.
Avoid moving the needle during injections as this may result in back flow.
Place a piece of wet gauze over the injection site.
Slowly retract the needle while holding the wet gauze in place.
Compress the injection site for 1 minute using firm finger pressure or instruments as weights.
Discard the wet gauze.
Hold the spleen with forceps in your left hand and the cautery in your right hand.
Cauterize the splenic ligaments to remove the spleen.
If bleeding is observed following splenectomy, place a few pieces of gauze at the site and add pressure for 3 min.
Once bleeding has stopped, remove the gauze.
Gently return the connective tissue into the peritoneal cavity after removing the spleen.
Suture the peritoneum once no further bleeding is observed.
Staple the skin layer with wound clips.
Topically administer 50 μL of 0.12% bupivacaine along the incision site using a 1 mL syringe.
Administer 300 μL of sterile saline via intraperitoneal injection to reduce dehydration from blood loss.
Place the mouse in a clean cage on top of an electrical heat pad and monitor until the animal has recovered from surgery.
Ensure that surgical tools are disinfected between mice by thoroughly wiping with 80% ethanol and F10sc veterinary disinfectant.
Provide sunflower seeds, peanut butter, and Hydrogel to aid with recovery.
Administer an additional dose of carprofen every 24 hours, for up to 72 hours.
Perform daily welfare checks.
Conduct detailed clinical monitoring at least twice a week.
Monitor weight loss as a key indicator of disease progression.
Perform daily clinical monitoring if ≥10% weight loss is observed.
Shave the surgical area and/or abdominal region of mice if needed for monitoring.
Monitor mice daily for reduced activity or unresponsiveness to surroundings.
Palpate the abdomen gently to detect liver metastases, noting any hard nodules indicative of KPC tumors.
Check for signs of jaundice such as pale eyes, ears, and feet.
Monitor for a hunched posture in mice.
Develop a monitoring plan for scoring clinical signs with guidance from the Animal Ethics Committee.
Euthanize mice by CO2 inhalation at the experimental endpoint or using an approved method.
Carefully remove the liver after euthanasia.
Rinse the liver 3 times in 1× PBS.
Weigh the liver as a surrogate measure of tumor burden.
Process the liver appropriately for downstream analysis (e.g., formalin fix, snap frozen, digestion for flow-cytometry).
Optimize the protocol to suit experimental needs based on study design and cancer cell line used.
Do not use mice for analysis if tumors are observed in organs other than the liver or at the incision site.
